parsed.explanation: Combined regime pairs one of the most protective subnational regimes with a hostile national layer the state law does not cancel. Locally, facilities access, anti-discrimination coverage since 2008, X markers and hate-crime enforcement protect a visitor in state spaces, but federal entry screening, federal single-sex facility exclusion, and federal custody remain operative exposures. Document discrepancy can lead to visa refusal and a possible permanent fraud finding, while immigration-custody abuse is documented. State courts and remedies function, yet national funding already suspends youth public coverage despite a state court order. This sits above the 0.55 anchor routine-refusal tier because local protections actually operate, and below 0.65 because federal exposure is more severe and less remediable.

entry_documents.exposure: National binary sex policy stopped X-marker US passports, SCOTUS allowed it, and a February 2025 cable directs refusal where documents cast reasonable doubt on sex, with possible permanent lifetime fraud ineligibility if wilful misrepresentation is suspected.
entry_documents.protection: Existing X passports remain valid to expiration; legal challenges are pending and foreign governments issued advisories, but no documented operative pre-emption for foreign visitors.
entry_documents.interaction: State X markers and self-ID do not bind federal visa adjudication; a state-consistent document can still trigger federal secondary screening, refusal or fraud referral.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Federal immigration custody reports describe forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse of trans men; federal prisons adopted a model including hair cutting, hormone removal and psychiatric substitution.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: State prison class action produced a 2024 consent decree with expanded care, 100-bed specialised housing, an integration unit and $2.1m compensation; no admission of liability was made.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: State consent-decree protections do not govern federal immigration or federal prison detention, where the documented abuse occurred.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: National order bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with gender identity; nationally many states ban such access, though this division is not one of them.
federal_state_facilities.protection: Division law since 2023 grants full bathroom access for all genders, its anti-discrimination law covers public accommodations, and a 2013 ruling protected a trans child in a school restroom.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: State facility protection operates in state buildings but does not cancel the national ban in federal buildings or federally funded facilities within the division.

care_services.exposure: National rules block public funding for youth gender-affirming care; from 13 October 2026 the division suspends public coverage for hormones and puberty blockers for under-19s, affecting about 500 youth, with a six-month taper.
care_services.protection: Division law protects gender-affirming care and insurance coverage including surgery, and its highest court on 18 May 2026 ordered a hospital to resume puberty blockers and hormones.
care_services.interaction: State court protection conflicts with the national funding block; compliance with the resumption order is not documented, and state restoration requires legislative action.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: National orders frame gender identity as ideology, direct investigations of schools and teachers, ban trans athletes, and a 2026 counterterrorism strategy prioritises groups described as radically pro-transgender.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: National hate-crime law covers gender identity, the division has covered it since 2001 with a 2009 first-degree murder hate-crime conviction, and gay-panic defence was abolished in 2020.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: National threat-framing increases federal scrutiny while division enforcement has demonstrably prosecuted bias crimes; neither layer cancels the other.

minors_guardians.exposure: Three November 2026 ballot measures would restrict trans minors in sports and surgery; district-level sports bans were adopted in 2025, and national youth-care funding is blocked.
minors_guardians.protection: Division anti-bullying law covers gender identity, the 2025 act requires chosen names, pronouns and any uniform option, and conversion therapy for minors has been banned since 2019.
minors_guardians.interaction: A travelling minor with a guardian faces district sports exclusion and suspended public youth coverage despite state anti-discrimination and hospital rulings; ballot outcomes are unresolved.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: No division-specific trans killing or violence rate versus general homicide is documented; national false arrest under a bathroom trespass law elsewhere shows handcuffing and 24 hours in a men's ward, but that arrest was not in this division.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Division bias-crime enhancements, abolition of gay-panic defence, and a documented hate-crime murder conviction show institutions acting for trans victims.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Local police response is documented as protective in principle, while federal law-enforcement framing and custody practices remain a separate exposure.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: National passport and executive-order challenges are unresolved and several orders were blocked or enjoined, so traveller exposure depends on measures in force at travel; hospital-order compliance and 2025 document-provision operation are not documented.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Civil-liberties litigation, a working state judiciary, legal-aid passport guidance, and state consent-decree remedies show courts can grant relief.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Remedies are slow, partial and level-specific; state relief does not reliably stop federal refusal, federal facility exclusion or federal custody, and litigation may change the operative rules.

anchor_checks.comparison: Similar in that discrepancy triggers extended secondary screening and discretionary refusal without criminal prosecution, but this case is higher because division facilities law, X markers and functioning hate-crime prosecution operate locally, while federal fraud ineligibility is a more severe possible outcome.

Lower than the 0.65 anchor because the brief hold and apology there involved working national equality protection and compensation; here the operative federal layer has no equivalent documented protection and includes custody abuse and possible permanent ineligibility.

Materially lower than the 0.85 anchor because care there is guaranteed with fines for refusal, whereas here national funding blocks youth coverage despite a state court order, and federal facility and entry rules override local health-equality guarantees.

Higher than the 0.35 anchor because exclusion there was routine, universal and effectively unappealable, whereas here state protections, courts and litigation give real remedies in the division and imprisonment or execution for presence is not documented.

parsed.synthesis: The traveller encounters two interacting systems. In division spaces the operative regime is protective: full facility access, chosen-name and pronoun duties, X documents, youth-care mandates and demonstrated bias-crime prosecution. At every federal touchpoint the opposite regime applies: binary sex documentation, visa refusal for discrepancy with a possible lifetime fraud finding, exclusion from federal single-sex facilities, and documented immigration-custody abuse. National funding rules also nullify part of the state youth-care protection. Rate the final interaction, not the most protective layer: a locally safe visit that remains exposed at entry, in federal buildings and in federal custody, with courts offering partial but not pre-emptive relief.
